outcome: The finiteness question — whether the odd greedy algorithm always terminates for every rational number with odd denominator — remains unresolved; the only post-window work found (Louwsma & Martino, 2025) characterizes special cases of fixed expansion length, which restricts a different, already-settled-to-exist question (which fractions have a length-2 expansion) rather than narrowing the open existence question of whether termination always occurs.
summary: The problem asks whether the odd greedy algorithm always terminates in finitely many steps for every rational number with odd denominator (Stein's question, also attributed to Selfridge and Graham). This is an existence/termination question in the sense of §3.1: it moves only when answered, not when more instances are verified or more special cases are classified. I found no result in the window (26 Jan 2024 to present) that resolves, bounds, or settles a genuine case of this question. The one pre-window item the triage found, Louwsma & Martino's 'Rational numbers with odd greedy expansion of fixed length' (arXiv:2309.07280, Sep 2023, single version, no updates), is unchanged and predates the window regardless. I found a follow-up by the same authors, 'Rational Numbers with Two-Term Odd Greedy Expansion,' published in INTEGERS vol. 25 (2025) and posted to Zenodo 28 May 2025 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15536292) — this is within the window. However, per its own and the earlier paper's framing, this work characterizes which fractions have an odd greedy expansion of exactly length 2 (a classification of a finite class of objects), not a restriction of the open termination question itself: it does not shrink the search space of potential counterexamples to termination, nor prove termination for any infinite subfamily left open by the conjecture. It is analogous to extending a record table rather than answering an existence question, so under §3.1's rule it does not count as a change to this problem's status. I also checked a superficially similar-sounding but unrelated 2025 paper on 'Irrationality of the reciprocal sum of doubly exponential sequences' (arXiv:2504.05933); its abstract confirms it addresses a different Erdős–Graham-type problem about doubly exponential sequences, not odd greedy expansions, and it is excluded as a related-but-different problem (§3.1). The Wikipedia article itself (fetched live for context, not as the frozen source) shows no updates past a 1999 citation and does not describe any resolution. I found no author, blog, or lab source connecting any AI system to this problem in any way; every search returned only pure human mathematical work (constructive/combinatorial classification arguments), so ai_role is 'none' with no basis_quote to offer.
competing_reading: One could argue the 2025 two-term paper is a 'case of the problem' under a looser reading — it does establish, for the specific finite set of fractions it characterizes, that their odd greedy expansion terminates (trivially, in 2 steps), which is technically an instance of 'this rational number has an odd greedy expansion.' But this is already known to be true for cofinitely many/most small-denominator fractions from prior computational verification (up to 922321), and characterizing which ones stop at exactly length 2 is bookkeeping about the algorithm's behavior on already-terminating instances, not progress toward ruling out or finding a non-terminating instance, which is what the open question is actually about. I classify this as no_change_found on the stated conjecture, consistent with §3.1's treatment of record/instance-type findings for existence questions.
what_would_settle_it: A proof that the odd greedy algorithm terminates for all rational numbers with odd denominator (or a rational number for which it is proven, by direct computation or otherwise, that the algorithm produces an infinite/non-terminating expansion) would resolve it. Short of that, a paper proving termination for a nontrivial infinite subfamily not previously known to terminate (e.g., all fractions with a given prime power denominator) would count as partial progress; the 2025 paper found does not do this.
